title: Care for the image (Leviticus Rabbah 34:3)
hookLine: Hillel goes to the bathhouse: caring for a body made in God's image is a mitzvah
tomorrow: can it ever be right to change someone's words?

cards: Self-care gets mocked sometimes: face masks, bubble baths, treat yourself. Pampering, not principle. So here's an odd little scene from Leviticus Rabbah.
Hillel finishes teaching, and as he walks off, his students follow. Rabbi, where are you going? To do a mitzvah.
Which mitzvah? To bathe in the bathhouse. Not a sick visit, not a lesson, not a meal for the poor.
A bath. The students stop. That's a mitzvah?

teach.b: Here's his answer. You know the statues of kings they set up in the theaters and circuses? The man in charge of them scrubs and washes them.
He gets paid for it, and he's even honored among the great of the kingdom.
And me, created in the image and likeness, as it says, "for in the image of God made He man"? How much more.
That's the rabbis' how-much-more argument, kal va-chomer: if the lesser thing deserves care, the greater one deserves more. That solves the puzzle. The Hebrew word is tselem, image.
In Hillel's world, an image of the king stood in public, and keeping it clean honored the king. So if a person is an image of God, washing that person isn't vanity.
It's upkeep on something royal. The thing to tell a friend tonight: Hillel compared his own body to a statue of the emperor, and won the argument. The same passage has a second scene.
Another day Hillel says he's going to do a kindness for a guest in his house. Do you have a guest every day? My poor soul, he says: here today, gone tomorrow.
Body as an image, soul as a guest.
Both get looked after. Sleep, water, a real meal: not a break from the holy work. Part of it.

how: Jewish law counts guarding your health as a duty, and teachers often bring Hillel's bathhouse story to show that caring for the body is part of serving God, not a distraction from it.

games.q: what does “care for the image” mean?
o: making a beautiful painting of a sacred scene
keeping statues of holy people clean and polished
looking after your body because it bears God's image

p: scrubbed, and the scrubber is honored
image, as in the image of God
his soul, here today, gone tomorrow

s: in this midrash, caring for your body is a distraction from holy things
Hillel calls a trip to the bathhouse a mitzvah.
Hillel compares himself to the statues of kings in the theaters
if they're scrubbed, how much more a person made in God's image.
in the same passage, Hillel calls his soul a guest
here today, gone tomorrow, so he looks after it.

games.q: your friend skips lunch every day to fit in more volunteer shifts. she says eating slowly would be selfish. by Hillel, what do you tell her?
o: 'you're right. serving others always comes before your own body.'
'just grab coffee; it keeps you going without wasting any time.'
'eat lunch. Hillel called a bath a mitzvah; your body is part of the work.'
games.why: for Hillel, caring for a body made in God's image is itself a mitzvah, upkeep on something royal, not time stolen from the holy.

practice: If you have water nearby, pour a glass, or cup some in your hands. Drink it slowly: notice the cold, the taste, where it goes.
Then sit back and let your shoulders drop, the way you'd set down something valuable you've been carrying carelessly all day.

wordCard.voice: Care for the image: Hillel's reason for a trip to the bathhouse. If kings' statues get scrubbed, how much more a body made in the image of God.

orig.note: Hebrew: image, as in 'in the image of God' (Genesis 1:27; 9:6).

carryVoice: Pocket this: care for the image. Hillel walked off to the bathhouse like he was going to synagogue.

sources.ref: Leviticus Rabbah 34:3 (Hillel goes to bathe: the statues of kings in theaters and circuses; and the soul as a guest in the body)
